body_markdown:
The world’s most valuable cars, like the world’s most valuable anything, tend to be very, very rare. McLaren F1? Just 106 of those. Ferrari 250 GTO? A scant 36 built. Bugatti Royale? Barely half a dozen. Rarity doesn’t always mean big prices, though. A[Swallow Doretti](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/swallow/doretti/1954/1954-swallow-doretti-base?id=aCn1I000000DQ8uSAG) , to pull out just one example, is a super-rare ’50s sports car with fewer than 300 built. But it’s also obscure, and most recent sales were for well under $100,000.


On the flip side, not everything that’s valuable is extremely rare. Sometimes provenance and style are enough to make a million-dollar car. Speaking of which, we recently went through our Price Guide to find which collector cars are currently worth $1M or more despite enjoying relatively high production numbers (in this case over 1000 units).


## [1954–57 Mercedes-Benz 300SL Gullwing](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes~benz/300sl/1955/1955-mercedes~benz-300sl-gullwing?id=aCn1I000000DVfQSAW)


Sandon Voelker


The 300SL has most of the ingredients that make up a high-dollar vintage automobile. There’s heritage, as it was developed from a winning race car (the W194) and was a successful competitor in its own right. It was also cutting-edge for its day, with a fuel-injected overhead cam engine, tube-frame chassis (which necessitated those famous doors), and independent suspension at all four corners. Then there was style. That the 300SL is a gorgeous thing has never been up for debate.


What the 300SL doesn’t have is extreme rarity. If the boys in Sindelfingen had only ever finished 100 copies of the 300SL, who knows how much they would be worth today. Luckily, they were much, much more productive than that. At a time when Ferrari’s annual production ran in the dozens, Mercedes-Benz was able to screw together 1400 Gullwings, with most of them selling in North America.


It was still an exclusive, expensive car in the ’50s. Jaguar, for example, sold nearly 10 times as many[XK120s](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/jaguar/xk_120/1950/1950-jaguar-xk_120-base?id=aCn1I000000CxGmSAK) , and for thousands of dollars less than the Mercedes. But for a seven-figure ’50s car, 1400 is a lot. Survivorship is also quite high in the 300SL world, so transactions are frequent. That kind of frequency provides a lot of valuable data on the top end of the classic car market, which is why we built and periodically check in on our[300SL Index](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/data-driven/what-mercedes-benz-300sl-sales-mean-for-the-collector-car-market/) . Gullwings have been million-dollar cars for over a decade, and currently #2 (excellent) values range from $1.65M to $1.95M depending on model year.


## [1958–64 Mercedes-Benz 300SL Roadster](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes~benz/300sl/1959/1959-mercedes~benz-300sl-base?id=aCn1I000000DEU9SAO)


Broad Arrow


By the second half of the ’50s, the 300SL Gullwing had proven itself on both race track and showroom floor, but instead of retiring it, the Germans updated it with a new Roadster version that was easier to live with and quicker. A redesigned tube frame allowed for lower sills and therefore conventional doors as well as roll-up windows. Power rose slightly, suspension was tweaked, and, in 1961, disc brakes were added. As a result, the Roadster sold even better than the Gullwing, with nearly 1900 built.


Today, the open and closed versions carry similar values. Condition #2 values range from $1.35M for early models to $1.9M for the final ’64 cars. Big price differentiators in the 300SL market include the optional Rudge wheels (+100K), factory-fitted luggage (+20K), and factory hardtops for Roadsters (+$75K).


## [1987–92 Ferrari F40](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/f40/1987/1987-ferrari-f40-base?id=aCn1I000000DGumSAG)


Broad Arrow


The last Ferrari launched while Enzo was still alive, the F40 was also a 40th-anniversary celebration for the company. It was famously analog and sparsely equipped, though its twin-turbocharged 2.9-liter V-8 and carbon/Kevlar body panels were highly advanced for the time.


Ferrari originally planned to build just 400 units, but the F40 also debuted at the height of a speculative[bubble](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-1980s-ferrari-bubble-crashed-the-collector-car-market-what-can-it-teach-us-today/) in collector cars, and Ferraris were the most highly prized. Flooded with more orders than anticipated, Ferrari ultimately built over 1300, all painted in Rosso Corsa. List price was around $400K, but they changed hands for much higher sums until that bubble popped in the early ’90s.


F40s are by far the most common of Ferrari’s “halo” models ([288 GTO](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/288_gto/1985/1985-ferrari-288_gto-base?id=aCn1I000000DGCySAO) , F40,[F50](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/f50/1995/1995-ferrari-f50-base?id=aCn1I000000DJtpSAG) ,[Enzo](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/enzo/2003/2003-ferrari-enzo-base?id=aCn1I000000DI6oSAG) ,[LaFerrari](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/laferrari/2014/2014-ferrari-laferrari-base?id=aCn1I000000CrUzSAK) , F80), but that doesn’t mean they’re cheap. They first crossed the million-dollar threshold in the mid-2010s, and hovered in the mid-$1M range for several years. Big demand for top-tier modern Ferraris has pushed F40s further in the 2020s, however, and the current condition #2 value in our price guide is a remarkable $4.5M.


## [2014–16 Ferrari 458 Speciale](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ferrari+458+speciale)


Broad Arrow


“Last-of” models tend to be coveted, and the 458’s collector cachet as the final naturally aspirated V-8 Ferrari is deeply rooted in this vein. The 458 also came at a time of expanded factory customization at Ferrari, so things like specialty paintwork and bespoke upholstery (both coveted by today’s collectors) became more common sights. Base-model 458 Italias went from used exotic to modern collector car at the beginning of the decade, and #2 values are nearly double what they were five years ago.


The 458 Speciale, though, is in a different league. This more powerful and more track-focused version cost about $290K when new, which was only about $50K more than the Italia, but today the Speciale is worth about three times as much. It crossed the $1M mark earlier this year, which is remarkable since this car isn’t that old, isn’t based on a top-shelf model, and isn’t that rare. Nobody quite knows *how* not that rare it is, but most sources point to about 1300 Speciales produced. The current #2 value is $1.1M.


## [2004–07 Porsche Carrera GT](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/carrera_gt/2004/2004-porsche-carrera_gt-base?id=aCn1I000000DV8tSAG)


Porsche


By halo hypercar standards, the Carrera GT is downright prolific. Porsche sold nearly 1300 of them, with about half of which came to North America. They’re more than three times as common as their main period nemesis, the Ferrari Enzo.


When new, a Carrera GT cost about half a million dollars, but that was 20 years ago. Since then, cars like the Carrera GT—stick-shift, naturally aspirated, non-hybrid, no driving aids—have all but ceased to exist, but in the collector car world there’s a clear appetite for them. This V-10 P-car has been one of the market’s biggest winners in this decade so far, when prices crossed the seven-figure threshold a few years ago, then corrected a bit, and then surged again during the exotic car boom of 2026. The current record for one is[$6,715,000](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/am26_r0191/2005-porsche-carrera-gt) , set apart by its unique color.
